title: What is Azure for .NET Developers
description: See how Azure services fit into ASP.NET Core and C# development workflows.

data.text: **Microsoft Azure** is a cloud platform that lets .NET developers host apps, store data, secure secrets, and monitor production systems without managing physical servers.

data.title: Benefits for C# developers
items: **First-class .NET SDKs** — Azure services ship with idiomatic C# client libraries
**Native Visual Studio tooling** — publish, debug, and monitor Azure apps from the IDE
**Hybrid and cloud flexibility** — run on Azure, on-premises, or both with the same C# code
**Enterprise-grade security and compliance** — built-in identity, encryption, and governance

data.title: C# First
data.text: Most Azure services expose async-first, Task-based C# client libraries. You will see `async Task` and `await` throughout this course because Azure operations are almost always network calls.

terms.definition: The management layer that creates, updates, and deletes Azure resources through APIs, PowerShell, or the Azure portal.
A set of NuGet packages that provides idiomatic C# client libraries for Azure services.

data.title: Call Azure Blob Storage from C#
data.content: Azure SDK methods use standard .NET patterns like async/await and `using` for disposables.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Azure provides managed services for hosting, storage, data, caching, and monitoring
Azure SDK for .NET gives you idiomatic C# client libraries
Visual Studio integrates deeply with Azure for development and deployment
Most Azure operations in C# are async because they call cloud services over HTTP
data.takeaway: Think of Azure as an extension of your C# toolbox: instead of building infrastructure yourself, you call Azure SDK methods from your existing code.
